The first major data ethics quandary I remember was the Cambridge Analytica scandal. I was just conscious enough to remember the craziness of the 2016 election, and this scandal emerged from that era. 

Here's a [link](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/03/17/us/politics/cambridge-analytica-trump-campaign.html?unlocked_article_code=1.TVE.-9dK.VPmT8KiVIhm2&smid=url-share.) to the story. 

We all know Trump likes to violate boundaries. And he loves recruiting others to violate those boundaries, too. This case is a perfect example of that. In 2014, Cambridge Analytica's founder Christopher Wylie said, "“Cambridge Analytica was supposed to be the arsenal of weapons to fight that [American] culture war.”" Obviously, this is a reference to the largely imaginary and irrelevant culture war Trump likes to invoke. The data science component involved Facebook, who worked in conjunction with an outside researcher, to provide millions of private profiles to the company. The company then received funding from MAGA elites to target these profiles with "psychographic" messaging before elections. Ultimately, 30 million profiles were harvested and manipulated in the years leading up to Trump's election. The ethical dilemma is the use of sensitive data to produce targeted messaging. On one hand, this is obviously a massive violation of privacy, especially because only 270,000 people even consented to have their data used. On the other hand, this is "standard practice" for Big Tech- targeted advertisements are as old as the Internet, and thus some of the burden falls on the users to remain vigilant. I'm more inclined to blame Big Tech...

Obviously, this example interfaces with Principle 1: "Use data to improve life for our users, customers, organizations, and communities." What this means is that the harvested data needs to have some tangible reasoning that will bring benefits to the subjects but also society as a whole. Using the Cambridge Analytica data for political messaging purposes is, to me, a violation of Principle 1. Donald Trump has objectively used his election to consolidate power for himself, not for the people. While his rule has incidentally benefitted society in some ways (mostly large corporations), from a utilitarian perspective, Principle 1 has been violated by the Cambridge data for the vast majority of Americans.

This example also addresses Principle 5: "Clearly identify the questions and objectives that drive each project and use to guide both planning and refinement." Basically, what this means is that the data needs to be put to *some* use, good or not. Obviously, the MAGA movement made work of their harvested data. The psychographic messaging was used to help Trump get elected, and Cambridge Analytica pitched their services to help MAGA from the start. Even though this is a violation of some other principles, it satisfies the premise of Principle 5.

Principle 9 was violated: "Consider carefully the ethical implications of choices we make when using data, and the impacts of our work on individuals and society." In other words, any gathered data has to be collected carefully, with regard to the far-reaching societal impacts, not just the narrow scope of the project. Cambridge Analytica violated this principle on two different levels. One, it helped bring about a destabilizing regime, which deepened polarization, poverty, and persecution of the marginalized. Societal consequences of Trump's reelection were largely ignored by the researchers at Cambridge. Second, it deepened the rift between Big Tech and the rest of society. Corporations and consumers are supposed to work together, and Cambridge manipulating millions of profiles violated that precept. 

Finally, Principle 11 was violated: "Protect the privacy and security of individuals represented in our data." Or, collected data has to be as anonymized as possible, with all identifying characteristics blotted out. The harvested profiles not only kept every single bit of information about their users, they were also scanned invasively to see who would benefit from psychographic manipulation. This is a clear violation of the individuals represented within the data; their personal characteristics were exposed *and* scrutinized without their knowledge or consent, and the data was sold to Facebook. In other words, it became a commodity, not a security. 

Cases like this matter a lot, and it's sad how little people in my generation seem to care. Everyone except the CEOs of Big Tech is negatively impacted by this case. It set a precedent that showed just how far corporations can go when it comes to violating our privacy. The elderly, immigrants, and other vulnerable populations are especially harmed, as they lack English-language digital literacy. Obviously, Big Tech and MAGA come out on top. What's especially scary is that this wasn't done because of profit. Rather, in a 1984esque twist, it was done for the pursuit of power. That should terrify us all.
